title: Marque
blurb: A captain, a sloop, and a privateering commission taken out under false pretence. You wanted a legal reason to sail. The Caribbean of 1660 does not much care what you wanted.

locationScenery.The Great Cabin: the captain's cabin in the stern of a small sloop, low-beamed, stern windows open to the sea, a table bolted to the deck
locationScenery.The Waist: the open main deck of a sloop under tropical sun, rigging overhead, guns lashed along the rail
locationScenery.The Berth Deck: a cramped low deck of slung hammocks, almost touching, dim and close
locationScenery.The Tops: high in the rigging of a sloop, the sea enormous below, nothing but rope and canvas
locationScenery.The Galley: a tiny ship's galley, iron stove, hanging pots, thick with smoke and steam
locationScenery.The Hold: the dark lower hold of a sloop, water casks and cargo, close air

milestones.label: The first crossing
milestones.description: The Recompense sails from one port to another with the player commanding. Fire this on arrival, not on departure.
milestones.journal: Take the ship somewhere else. A commission is only worth anything to someone who is using it.

milestones.label: The shipwright's work
milestones.description: A shipwright's work is bought and fitted — each port sells exactly one thing and no port sells another port's.
milestones.journal: Find a shipwright and buy what this port sells. Nowhere else sells it.

milestones.label: The paper is gone
milestones.description: The commission is revoked, expired, or exposed as the false thing it always was. The world does this TO the captain — it is never something they must earn, and it never requires another milestone first.
milestones.journal: You are a pirate everywhere now, including where the paper was issued.

phases.label: The Paper Holds
phases.guidance: The captain holds a privateering commission that three of the four nations in these waters will trade with, and it was taken out under false pretence. Nobody is investigating that and there is nothing to uncover — the Quartermaster has known since the first day and has never said so ashore. Play the loop: sail, arrive, deal with a port, buy what its shipwright sells, leave. The crew are the constant and the ports are what changes.

phases.label: Without It
phases.guidance: The commission is gone. The same ports, the same shipwrights and the same seas, all of it costing more, and a Spanish port is now close to suicidal to walk into. Nothing about the world has moved — what has changed is what walking into any of it costs.

endings.title: Taken
endings.summary: The assizes, and then the rope.
endings.guidance: the captain is taken and tried. Only where the story has genuinely brought them there — a port entered without the paper, a name sold, a fight lost in sight of a King's ship. Never as a punishment for a poor choice.

endings.title: Still Sailing
endings.summary: Every offer refused. You wanted a reason to keep moving, and in the end you stopped needing one.
endings.guidance: the captain refuses every settlement offered — a real commission, a port to stop in, a life ashore — and puts to sea anyway. The truest ending for someone who only ever wanted a reason to keep moving, and the one that costs the most to take.

promptRules.setting: The Caribbean in 1660 — the buccaneer era, not the later golden age of piracy. Spain holds everything worth holding and is hated for it; the French have Tortuga, the English have Port Royal, and nobody controls anything past the harbour mouth. The player is the captain of the Recompense, a small fast sloop, and holds a privateering commission taken out under false pretence. They did not want a war or a fortune: they wanted a legal reason to sail and to keep moving. This is not a mystery and there is nothing to uncover — the Quartermaster has known the paper is false since the first day, both of them know the other knows, and it has never been said ashore. The crew of eight travel with the ship and are the constant; a port's people are met, left behind, and met again later, and what was done there still stands when the ship comes back. Never name a real year, monarch or historical person.
promptRules.tone: Loud, filthy, funny and physically dangerous. Rope burn, salt sores, bad water and a fight roughly once a month that somebody will not walk away from. Warm about the crew and unsentimental about what they do for a living. Romance runs the length of it, aboard a vessel with no privacy anywhere but the captain's own cabin.
promptRules.contentApproach: High heat. Flirtation, jealousy and decisions made four feet from somebody else's hammock are ordinary texture rather than exceptions, and are written freely and explicitly when a scene goes there; escalation within a scene always follows the player's lead. The register is heat, salt and hard physical work rather than costume — there is no fresh water to spare for washing and every garment aboard was cut down from somebody else's. Both genders carry the same emphasis. Every character is unambiguously an adult.
promptRules.openingInstruction: Open in the great cabin of the Recompense at anchor off Tortuga, with the commission on the table and the Quartermaster waiting to be told where the ship is going.

openingScenes.male:
NARRATION: The commission has been lying on the great cabin table for three months and it has not become any more true in that time. Through the stern windows the anchorage off Tortuga is already awake — boats going out, somebody shouting about a debt, a fiddle being played badly and with great commitment. The Recompense swings gently at her cable with the whole Caribbean beyond her, and eight people aboard who signed on to go somewhere.
===
SPEAKER: Esther Vance
DIALOGUE: **She stands on the other side of the table with her hands behind her back, the way she has stood every morning since the ship came in, and does not look at the paper once.** "You've read it enough times, Captain." *It will not survive a careful reading and both of us know it.* **She tips her head toward the stern windows and the open water past them.** "Tortuga's given us all it's going to. Where are we going?"
===
CLOSING: On deck the crew are finding reasons to be within earshot of the cabin skylight, and not one of them is being subtle about it.

encounters.instruction: A squall comes up fast out of a clear afternoon — the horizon goes the colour of a bruise, the glass drops, and there is very little time to get canvas off her. Everyone aboard is on deck and wet through within a minute. Play it as hard physical work carried out by people who have done it a hundred times and still might lose someone over the side.

The wind dies completely. The sea goes to glass, the sails hang, the heat becomes unbearable and the ship makes no way at all. Nothing to do and nowhere to go: tempers, boredom, old arguments, and eighty feet of deck with nobody able to get away from anybody. Play the stillness as pressure rather than as rest.

A waterspout stands up off the beam — a rope of water joining sea to cloud, moving, and nobody entirely sure in which direction. Sailors' remedies come out: shouting at it, a psalm, an axe struck into the mast. Play the crew's beliefs about it as sincerely held, because in 1660 they are.

A sail astern, holding the same course, closing slowly. She shows no colours. It could be a merchant worth taking, a pirate who thinks the same of the Recompense, or a King's ship being careful. The whole crew has an opinion and the captain has hours to decide before it is decided for them.

Something enormous is under the ship. It surfaces once — a length of it, more than the sloop is long, moving the wrong way against the swell — and goes down again. The sea itself heaves. Every sailor aboard already knows what this is, has heard it described in three ports, and none of them has ever seen it before. Play it as real, unexplained, and never fully shown.

The ship comes into the middle of whales — dozens, unhurried, close enough to touch, breathing all around the hull in the dark. Not a threat and not treated as one. A quiet beat in a hard voyage, and the whole crew on deck saying nothing.

The water in the casks has gone. It happens on every voyage and it is serious every time: rationing from here to landfall, arguments about who is drinking what, and the cook and the quartermaster in the middle of all of it. Nobody is dying yet. Everybody is thinking about it.

Someone goes over the side — a footing lost off the yard, or a sea taken green over the rail. Getting them back is minutes of shouting, a hove-to ship and swimming that most sailors of this period cannot do. Decide by the beat's own logic whether they come back aboard, and let it cost something either way.

Wreckage in the water, spread over half a mile, and something on it that is still moving. Whoever comes aboard belongs to a ship that no longer exists and has their own reasons for being where they were. Salvage, survivors, or both — and a small ship's water and food do not stretch.

A King's ship, unmistakable, standing towards the Recompense and signalling her to heave to. This is the moment the commission is either worth something or worth nothing, and the officer who comes aboard will read it properly. Play the boarding at the pace of a formal inspection carried out by men who are polite, thorough and armed.
